unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Unit 10 is the last unit of Year 4, and it gathers up the whole year. You revise thirty words from Units 1 to 8, from mail and moisture to labourer, terrified and equipment. Six grammar workshops bring back the present, past and future forms, the modal verbs, the question shapes, the comparisons and the joining words. Then you curate six pages, build a display board called My English Voice, and present it at the Year 4 Exhibition, just as Amal does in this unit's story.
unit.learningPath:
Read "Amal's English Voice", the Exhibition brief, the poem "Nine Rooms" and the two listening texts, then answer the twelve comprehension questions.
Revise the thirty review words and build your eight-box word map, unit by unit.
Work through the six cumulative grammar workshops, one at a time and never all at once.
Curate six pages, write the captions, and build the display board.
If you have access to live teacher sessions, rehearse across them and deliver your two-minute Exhibition talk there — this is optional. If you are learning independently, rehearse and record your two-minute Exhibition talk on your own or with your family instead.
Finish with the capstone quiz, the portfolio assignment and your Grade 5 reflection.
howToUse: This is your capstone: one big project that uses everything you learned this year. There is no video — start by reading about the project.
In Reading there are five texts: the story “Amal's English Voice”, the Exhibition project brief, the poem “Nine Rooms”, and two listening texts — “Planning the Exhibition” and “Exhibition Evening”.
In Writing you build your own exhibition: choose six pages of your best work, write a caption for each, and put together the display board.
In Speaking you practise a two-minute Exhibition talk. If you have no live sessions, record it on your own or with your family.
The Final course quiz is on this page, after every section has a tick. It is extra — it does not lock the unit.

readings.title: Amal's English Voice
readings.setting: The Year 4 classroom and Amal's home
readings.passageScript:
It was the last Monday of Year 4. Teacher Yasmin placed one thick blue folder on every desk.
"Everything you have written this year is inside," she said. "Choose the six pages that carry your own English voice."
Amal opened her folder and found her Unit 1 report about Omar at the post counter. She had asked him why mail still matters, and he had answered, "A letter can make someone feel remembered."
Behind it sat her weather poster from Unit 2, with a tornado drawn in thick grey pencil. Beside that lay her food-safety leaflet from Unit 3.
"I remember the bitter sandwich," laughed her friend Nora. "You wrote that whole leaflet after Doctor Sarah told you to check your food."
Amal turned another page. Unit 5 held the map she had drawn of the spiral cave. Unit 6 held her parade sign for Elena the engineer. Unit 8 held the attic list, written in careful columns: equipment, folder, telescope.
Her older brother Adam had called the attic list her dullest page. Amal was doubtful about it too, and for one moment she nearly slid it into the bin.
Then she read her own last line again: "We wore gloves and masks, because the attic had been closed for eleven years."
She kept it. It was the first sentence she had ever written with two clauses joined properly.
"Six pages, Amal," called Teacher Yasmin. "And one two-minute talk for the Exhibition on Friday."
Amal wrote her title at the top of a clean sheet: My English Voice.
That evening she read the six pages aloud at the kitchen table. Her younger sister Mina listened without moving. Idris asked what a canyon was, and Amal explained it without opening the dictionary once.
Grandma Hana put down her tea. "In Unit 1 you read to me one word at a time," she said. "Tonight you read to me like somebody who owns the words."
Amal wrote that down, because she wanted to use it on Friday.
On Friday morning she felt nervous, and she said so out loud. Nora was nervous too.
"Speak slowly and look at one kind face," said Teacher Yasmin. "That is all a presenter has to do."
Amal stood beside her display, took one steady breath, and began. "Good evening. My name is Amal, and this is my English voice."

readings.title: The Year 4 Exhibition: Project Brief
readings.setting: The Year 4 classroom and the school hall
readings.passageScript:
The Year 4 Exhibition closes your English year. It has four parts, and you complete them in order.

Part 1: Choose your six pages. Take them from at least five different units. Your set must show reading, writing, speaking and new words.

Part 2: Build your display board. Write two paragraphs on every page. Add one picture and one clear label to each page. Print your name and your class on the front.

Part 3: Prepare your talk. It lasts two minutes. Open with your name, present three pages, then answer two questions from the audience.

Part 4: Write your reflection. Name one thing that was genuinely hard this year, one thing that improved, and one goal for Grade 5.

Deadlines. Pages chosen by Tuesday. Board finished by Thursday. Talk rehearsed with a partner by Thursday evening. The Exhibition opens on Friday at five o'clock in the school hall.

Marks. Sixteen marks for the board, sixteen for the talk, sixteen for your corrected draft, and sixteen for your reflection.

One rule matters more than the rest: every page must be your own work, written in your own English voice.

readings.title: A Poem: Nine Rooms
readings.setting: The school hall on the last Monday of Year 4
readings.passageScript:
Nine rooms stood open down our Year 4 hall,
and I walked into every single one.

Room One held the mail and the market till,
where Omar weighed each parcel with such care.

Room Two was weather: moisture, hail and cloud,
one paper tornado spinning in the tent.

Room Three smelled of rice and lamb and spice,
and taught me how to keep my sandwich safe.

Room Four was full of service and of news,
that library which travelled on a cart.

Room Five began to gallop and to race,
then curled into a spiral underground.

Room Six was crowded: caretaker and judge,
one carpenter, one labourer, one friend.

Room Seven held the feelings I had hidden,
the nervous ones, the doubtful and the proud.

Room Eight kept old equipment in a folder,
one telescope that pulled the stars down close.

Room Nine was every station, every plan,
the far horizon, and the road back home.

Nine rooms, one hall, one year, one growing voice,
and now I hold the key to all of them.

grammar.title: Present Forms Review: Habits Now and Actions Now
grammar.origin: Ehel Grade 4 capstone authored from the rebuilt Units 1-9
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: Unit 1 taught the present simple with adverbs such as usually and never. Unit 2 used the present simple for science facts, Unit 4 for information writing, and Unit 6 for everyday jobs. Units 2 and 7 added the present continuous. The present simple tells what is normally true, while the present continuous tells what is happening at this moment.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Present simple, third person, adds -s: "The caretaker opens the hall at seven."
Adverbs of frequency stand before the main verb: "Omar usually sorts the mail first."
With the verb to be, the adverb comes after it: "Nora is always early."
Present continuous is am, is or are plus the -ing form: "Elena is checking the plans right now."
Science facts stay in the present simple: "Rice grows in wet fields."
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often drop the -s and write "The caretaker open the hall at seven." The subject is one person, so the verb needs its -s ending.
grammar.memoryTip: Ask yourself one question: is this true every week, or true only right now? Every week takes the present simple.
grammar.practice: Part A: write the present simple. | The carpenter (mend) the market stall every Saturday. | Grandma Hana always (wash) the rice twice. | Part B: write the present continuous. | Look at the hall now. Teacher Yasmin (count) the chairs. | Do not disturb Leo. He (rehearse) his two-minute talk. Self-check: Part A answers are mends and washes; Part B answers are is counting and is rehearsing.

grammar.title: Past Forms Review: Telling What Already Happened
grammar.origin: Ehel Grade 4 capstone authored from the rebuilt Units 1-9
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: Units 1, 5 and 8 taught the past simple, Unit 6 added the past continuous, and Unit 7 introduced the present perfect for life experience. The past simple names one finished moment, the past continuous sets the longer action around it, and the present perfect says that something has happened at some time in your life.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Regular verbs add -ed: deliver becomes delivered, gallop becomes galloped.
Irregular verbs change shape: build becomes built, take becomes took, write becomes wrote.
Past continuous is was or were plus the -ing form: "Leo was measuring the wall when the bell rang."
Present perfect is have or has plus the past participle: "I have presented twice this year."
Negatives use did not plus the plain verb: "We did not finish the board on Tuesday."
grammar.commonMistake: After did, learners keep the -ed and write "We did not finished the board." The helper did already carries the past, so the main verb stays plain.
grammar.memoryTip: Put the word yesterday at the front of your sentence. If yesterday fits, you need the past simple, not the present perfect.
grammar.practice: Part A: write the past simple. | Sami (deliver) the invitations on Tuesday morning. | Amal (take) one slow breath before she began. | Part B: choose the past continuous or the present perfect. | Nora (wipe) the moisture off the window when Maya arrived. | Amal (visit) the travelling library many times since Unit 4. Self-check: Part A answers are delivered and took; Part B answers are was wiping and has visited.

grammar.title: Plans, Promises and Modal Verbs From Nine Units
grammar.origin: Ehel Grade 4 capstone authored from the rebuilt Units 1-9
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: Unit 9 taught going to and would like to, Unit 8 taught will for promises and have to for obligation, Unit 3 taught must and might, Unit 6 taught should and mustn't, and Units 2 and 5 taught can. Each form carries a different strength, so choosing the right one matters more than knowing the list.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Going to states an arranged plan: "We are going to open the hall at five."
Will makes an on-the-spot promise: "I will bring the folder tomorrow."
Would like to states a wish politely: "Nora would like to present second."
Have to and must state an obligation: "Every visitor has to sign the book."
Should gives advice and mustn't gives a rule: "You should rehearse twice. You mustn't run in the hall."
Can states ability or permission: "Idris can read the whole page now."
grammar.commonMistake: Learners sometimes write "I will going to present first." One verb group holds one future form only, so keep will, or keep going to, and remove the other.
grammar.memoryTip: Ask who decided, and when. If the plan was decided earlier, use going to. If you decide while you are speaking, use will.
grammar.practice: Part A: complete with going to, will or would like to. | The Exhibition ______ open at five o'clock on Friday. | "That board is heavy. I ______ carry it for you," said Adam. | Part B: complete with have to, should or mustn't. | Every learner ______ wear gloves before entering the dusty attic. | You ______ leave your folder on the floor, where somebody may tread on it. Self-check: Part A answers are is going to open and will carry; Part B answers are has to wear and mustn't leave.

grammar.title: Asking Well: Questions, Short Answers and Question Tags

grammar.explanation: Unit 1 taught interview questions, Units 2 and 3 taught the Wh- and Yes/No forms, Unit 6 added question words for reporting, Unit 7 practised question forms about feelings, and Unit 9 added question tags. At the Exhibition you must both ask and answer, so every one of these comes back together.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Wh- questions begin with the question word, then the helper, then the subject: "Where did Leo measure the wall?"
Yes/No questions begin with the helper: "Did Sami deliver the invitations?"
Short answers repeat the helper only: "Yes, he did." or "No, he did not."
Question tags flip the verb: one positive sentence takes the negative tag, and one negative sentence takes the positive tag.
Examples: "We are presenting on Friday, aren't we?" and "Nora isn't nervous, is she?"

grammar.memoryTip: Say the sentence, then say the opposite of its helper out loud. That opposite is nearly always the tag you need.

grammar.explanation: Unit 2 taught comparative and superlative adjectives, Unit 5 taught adjective and noun phrases with adverbs of manner, Unit 6 added strong verbs and similes, and Unit 9 added comparative adverbs. Precise description is what turns one plain board into the board a visitor remembers.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Short adjectives add -er and -est: fast, faster, the fastest.
Longer adjectives use more and the most: careful, more careful, the most careful.
Adverbs of manner usually end in -ly: "Nora spoke calmly and clearly."
Comparative adverbs use more: "Amal reads more fluently than she did in Unit 1."
Similes compare with like or as: "The hall was as quiet as the attic."

grammar.memoryTip: Count the syllables in the adjective. One or two short syllables usually take -er, and three or more take the word more.

Self-check: Part A answers are stronger and the most powerful; the Part B adverb is carefully. The simile is open-ended, so check that your own answer uses like or as, for example "like a corkscrew" or "like a coiled snake."

grammar.origin: Ehel Grade 4 capstone authored from the rebuilt Units 1-9

grammar.explanation: Unit 8 taught relative clauses with who, that and which, Unit 4 taught the passive and the sequence connectives, Unit 1 taught conjunctions, Unit 5 taught sequencing in the how-to guide, and every unit asked you to proofread. Relative clauses add information about people: "Elena is the engineer who built the bridge."

grammar.commonMistake: Learners often join two whole sentences with only a comma, which leaves the reader with nowhere to stop. Use a full stop, or add a joining word such as because or although.

teacherNotes.noteType: Capstone provenance, grammar answer key, moderation and device safety
teacherNotes.note:
Where the revision comes from. Every review item in this capstone is traceable to a unit the class has already finished. The thirty words are Units 1 to 8: mail, language, citizen and agree from Unit 1; breath, sweat, moisture and surface from Unit 2; sandwich, lamb, rice and spice from Unit 3; service, deliver, information and thought from Unit 4; gallop, accelerate, proceed and spiral from Unit 5; caretaker, carpenter, labourer and engineer from Unit 6; nervous, anxious, terrified and doubtful from Unit 7; equipment and folder from Unit 8. Unit 9 supplies no headword, because the vocabulary slots for this unit were fixed before it was written; Unit 9 is revised instead through the question tags and future forms in Grammar 3 and Grammar 4, the travel couplet in the poem, and the planning talk in the Reading section.
The six grammar workshops revise, in order: Workshop 1 the present simple, adverbs of frequency and the present continuous from Units 1, 2, 4, 6 and 7; Workshop 2 the past simple, past continuous and present perfect from Units 1, 5, 6, 7 and 8; Workshop 3 will, going to, would like to, can, must, should, mustn't and have to from Units 2, 3, 5, 6, 8 and 9; Workshop 4 Wh- questions, Yes/No questions, short answers and question tags from Units 1, 2, 3, 6, 7 and 9; Workshop 5 comparatives, superlatives, adjective and noun phrases, adverbs of manner and similes from Units 2, 5, 6 and 9; Workshop 6 relative clauses, the passive, connectives, imperatives and proofreading from Units 1, 4, 5, 8 and 9.
Grammar workshop answer key. Workshop 1: mends, washes, is counting, is rehearsing. Workshop 2: delivered, took, was wiping, has visited. Workshop 3: is going to, will, has to, mustn't. Workshop 4: When did Leo measure the wall? Did the caretaker open the hall early? haven't you? was she? Workshop 5: stronger, most powerful, carefully, and accept any simile that compares the staircase to something that curls. Workshop 6: Karim is the tradesperson who mended our display stand. This is the report that won the Unit 1 writing contest. The hall was opened at four o'clock by the caretaker. Teacher Yasmin counted every chair before the visitors arrived. The last item is deliberately printed without capitals so that learners have something real to proofread.
Moderation. Conference at each of the six milestones rather than only at the end, and leave the page choices in the child's hands. Mark the board and the recording with the shared Grade 4 rubrics, and record one specific Grade 5 transition target for every learner.
Device safety and inclusion. Keep an adult present whenever a child records audio or works with the AI tutor, and never leave a young learner alone with the device. Offer spoken, drawn or written responses so that a child who finds writing hard can still show a full year of progress. The private Thursday rehearsal in the listening text is a real offer: make it available to any child who asks. Reflection can surface genuine disappointment, so agree in advance who the child may talk to, and always name one true strength before you name a target.

Reading, writing, speaking and vocabulary evidence must all be present somewhere in the set. If one learner has six pages from three units, ask them to swap two rather than add a seventh page.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "My English Voice: Grade 4 Capstone" — new words, a grammar focus, and a story. See exactly what they will practise below.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 8-9 years old and is building on English they already know. So YOU lead this unit alongside them — a teacher in class or a parent at home.

Work in short, regular sessions rather than one long one. Reading together, saying words out loud, and playing with the grammar patterns matter more than getting every answer right first time.

This guide tells you what the unit covers and how to go through it together. The learner's own pages (Reading & story, Grammar, Activities) are what your child works through on screen.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
The AI Tutor is there for extra practice and conversation — a grown-up should still be nearby, especially the first few times.

Ask the tutor to say a word slowly so your child can copy it: "Please say the word 'mail' slowly."

Ask it to make up a short question using this unit's words, or to listen to your child's sentence and say if it sounds right.

Ask it for one more practice question if your child wants to keep going after the unit is finished.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for teaching this unit
sections.body:
Keep sessions short and positive. Stop while it is still enjoyable, not after it has become a chore.

Say new words and example sentences out loud yourselves — hearing English spoken, not just reading it, is what builds confidence.

Let your child make mistakes without worrying. Gently model the correct version rather than correcting every slip.

Praise effort and progress, not just correct answers — confidence carries a learner further than perfect grammar at this stage.

sections.title: What Your Child Will Be Able to Do
items: Revise the thirty Grade 4 review words from Units 1 to 8 and use them accurately in speech and writing.

Plan, draft and publish a six-page display board that suits a real Exhibition audience.
Deliver a two-minute Exhibition talk and answer audience questions clearly and politely.
Evaluate your own and a partner's work, proofread the final draft, and set one Grade 5 goal.

sections.title: How to Teach This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
Repeat this simple shape over one or two short sessions:

1. Warm-up (2-3 min)
Say hello in English together and ask what your child remembers from the last unit.

2. Learn the words (5-10 min)
Go through Grade 4 Review Words, a few words at a time. Say each word, then have your child repeat it and use it in a short sentence.

3. Grammar and practice (5-10 min)
Look at "Present Forms Review: Habits Now and Actions Now" together and try a few lines of its practice out loud.

4. Story and listening time (5 min)
Read or listen to "Amal's English Voice" together, and enjoy "Planning the Exhibition" too.

5. Activity time (5-10 min)
Sit with your child and do "Activities 1 — Curate Six Pages From Nine Units" together, reading each instruction aloud for them if needed.

6. Wrap-up (2 min)
Ask what they learned today and celebrate with a “Well done!”

sections.body: You do not need a test. Just watch for these as you go through the unit together:

Twelve comprehension answers quoting details from the named passage, and the two reading-comprehension quiz items.
The six grammar workshop practices, the card sort in Activities 3, and the rewritten Unit 1 interview report.
The curated six pages, the six captions, the information page with its bulleted facts, and the finished standing board.
The recorded two-minute talk, the rehearsal circle feedback sheets, and four answered visitor questions.
Three written peer suggestions, the corrected draft showing two acted-upon changes, and the four-sentence reflection with its goal.
